bib.title: ALE-Bench: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Objective-Driven Algorithm Engineering

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "ALE-Bench: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Objective-Driven Algorithm Engineering", Imajuku, Horie, Iwata, Aoki, Takahashi, Akiba. Venue as printed: "39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025) Track on Datasets and Benchmarks"; arXiv:2506.09050v2, 6 Oct 2025. First author (Imajuku): "Sakana AI, Japan". Other affiliations printed: The University of Tokyo; AtCoder.

COVERAGE: 46 of 46 pages, 167,606 of 167,606 chars. References (pp. 11-13) and the NeurIPS checklist boilerplate (pp. 14-20) skimmed; the checklist answers were read. Library lists and prompt templates (pp. 30-40) read lightly. Figures were read from captions and axis text only, not viewed.

CLAIMS (most important first)

1. How grading works: the private score (usually the sum over hidden test cases) is placed on the original human contest leaderboard to give a rank, and the rank is converted to an Elo-like "performance" (roughly 0-3500).
   - number: none
   - setup: 40 AtCoder Heuristic Contest problems (10 in the lite subset); one private evaluation per session.
   - quote: "our benchmark approximates performance based solely on the agent's equivalent rank" (p26)
   - Ties are linearly interpolated. For some problems (ahc016/017/025), normalised scores are recomputed against all humans.

2. The authors recommend average performance over rating, because rating overstates AI.
   - number: none
   - quote: "a single exceptionally high performance can disproportionately inflate an AI's rating" (p5); "Rating is designed to reward high scores without penalizing low ones" (p8)

3. Average versus consistency: the best iterative-refinement model is top 11.8% by rating but only top 22.3% by average performance, with a per-problem profile like much lower-rated humans.
   - number: rating 2104 (11.8%); average performance 1520 (22.3%)
   - setup: o4-mini-high, C++20, 4-hour iterative refinement, full 40 problems, single run.
   - quote: "o4-mini-high achieved ≥1600 performance in 32.5% of problems; this is below the 56.2% average for humans in the same band and is closer to the 33.9% average for users rated 1600–1700" (p8)
   - At the top end it matches the band: ≥2400 on "5.0% of problems, while humans in this band averaged 4.0%" (p8).

4. One-shot models sit below the human average.
   - number: best is o3-high at 1044 against a human average of 1260
   - setup: C++20, up to five generations only to fix errors, 40 problems.
   - quote: "o3-high 1116 946 1044 97.5 5.0 0.0 1456 43.2" and "Human Average 1252 1257 1260 95.7 23.8 8.5 1414" (p7); "never reached 2000" (p6)

5. Iterative refinement with public-test feedback raised every model tested.
   - number: more than 400 points
   - setup: 4 models, 4 hours (or the contest duration if shorter), full set.
   - quote: "Average performance improved by over 400 points across all models" (p7)

6. Refinement beat the best of 150 independent one-shot samples.
   - number: about 300 points or more
   - setup: o4-mini-high, only the 6 problems where it had already scored ≥2000 (a selected set).
   - quote: "the performance deficit being approximately 300 points or more" (p9)

7. Scaffolding: a general agent did not help, and tree search helped a lot at roughly nine times the cost.
   - number: ALE-Agent 1167 to 1264 to 1879; cost $7.64 to $100.33 per problem; OpenHands 903
   - setup: lite subset (10 problems), Gemini 2.5 Pro, 4 hours, single run.
   - quote: "Base 1121 1213 1167 56.9 ... 7.64"; "+ Method 1&2 2285 1474 1879 6.8 100.0 70.0 30.0 20.0 2222 8.6 100.33 0.113"; OpenHands Gemini 2.5 Pro "726 1080 903 82.8" (p9)
   - "Cost data suggest OpenHands often exited prematurely" (p8). ALE-Agent generated "approximately 1000" codes (p9).

8. Budget by wall-clock time versus by number of calls changes the comparison.
   - number: about 60 versus about 300 generations in four hours
   - quote: "DeepSeek-R1 generated approximately 60 codes in four hours, whereas GPT-4.1-mini produced around 300" (p41)
   - Table A8 (p46): GPT-4.1 mini 924 at 10 calls against DeepSeek-R1 1107, but 1218 against 1221 at the end.

9. Contamination and plagiarism handling.
   - number: 12 programs reviewed
   - quote: "No model exhibited notable performance changes around its cutoff" (p9); "manually reviewed all 12 AI-generated programs that achieved ≥2000 performance" (p10)
   - The rules forbid visiting pages containing "AtCoder", "AHC" or the problem name (pp. 27-28).

10. Repeats and intervals: the main results are single runs, with one five-run appendix check on the one-shot setting.
    - number: five runs, 95% CI
    - quote: "we report the evaluation results of a single run for each model" (p16); "o3-high 1057.81 ± 46.74" (Table A7a, p46)

11. Lite versus full subset.
    - number: Pearson r = 0.9174, slope about 0.7
    - setup: 73 results.
    - quote: "Pearson's r = 0.9174"; "directly comparing across versions is not recommended" (p42)

LIMITS
- Conceded by the authors: single runs ("Limited statistical robustness", p43); only 40 problems; the sandbox is not an exact replica of AtCoder's; newer algorithms are now available for old contests; the problems are public. Image input, visualisers and tool use are largely untested.
- Not shown:
  - No time budget beyond 4 hours was tested. Long contests (200-367 hours for humans) were capped at 4 hours for AI, so the short-versus-long gap is confounded with budget.
  - The contamination check is a visual scatter with no statistical test. The plagiarism check was done by one author.
  - There are no intervals on the iterative or scaffolding results. The ALE-Agent ablation is 10 problems, one run, one model.
  - Rating depends on the subset: the same o4-mini-high run is 2104 (11.8%) on the full set and 1386 (48.2%) on lite.
  - The Wilcoxon p-values sit at 0.031, which looks like the floor for n=5 (my inference; the paper does not state the pairing unit).
  - A single time-limit failure zeroes a problem (Gemini 2.5 Pro scored -70 on ahc020).
- Dated: the models are from April-May 2025.

BUILDS ON: AtCoder rating system ver. 1.00 (2019) and AHC rating system ver. 2 (2025); Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023); OpenHands (Wang et al., 2025); MLE-bench (Chan et al., 2024); FunSearch-style work on score-based contests (Veličković et al., 2024); Kwa et al., 2025 on long tasks.

CODE: none worth keeping. The ALE-Agent search is best-first with "a beam of k = 30 child nodes" (p29).

FIGURES: Figure 5, p8, "Trends in public score and code file size in the iterative-refinement setting". One model's best-so-far public score climbs across about 160 generations while the code grows, which shows the refinement trajectory at a glance. Judged from the caption and axis text; I did not view the image.

PROBLEMS
- Prompt listings are extracted letter-spaced. Plots come through as axis ticks only; the Figure A5 search tree is unreadable as text.
- The PDF contains prompt templates addressed to LLM contestants (pp. 30-40). I treated them as data and followed none.
- Internal slips in the paper:
  - C.4 calls the full-version scaffolding table "Table 4"; it is Table A5.
  - C.3 points to "Section 5.2" for the human comparison; it is in 5.4.
  - The checklist and C.6 say single runs, while C.5.1 reports five.
  - The Human Average overall (1260) exceeds both its short (1252) and long (1257) parts, unexplained.
